title: Revealing non-trivial information structures in aneural biological tissues via functional connectivity
author: Blackiston, Dromiack, Grasso and colleagues, including Michael Levin
claim: Calcium imaging in six frog epidermal organoids reveals structured patterns of functional connectivity before and after injury. Methods used for neural tissue can also investigate non-neural coordination.
limit: Functional connectivity is a statistical relationship. Neither network structure nor coordinated repair establishes subjective experience. The sample is small.
use: Read the author summary and inspect Figure 1. Separate a measured signal, an inferred network and a claim about mind.
review: Abstract and publication record checked

title: Mind Everywhere — Part One
author: Michael Levin and David B. Resnik
claim: Proposes treating goal-directedness and cognition as testable approaches to interacting with biological systems across scales.
limit: This is a conceptual framework drawing on experiments, not an experiment establishing that all matter has experience.
use: Compare an operational definition of cognition with an account of conscious experience.
access: Abstract open; full text may require library access
review: Abstract and publication record checked

title: Ingressing Minds: Causal, Non-Physical Patterns In-Form Natural, Synthetic, and Hybrid Embodiments
author: Michael Levin
claim: A theoretical proposal about patterns and their embodiment in natural and engineered systems.
limit: Speculative philosophical framework. Biological findings do not independently establish its non-physical ontology.
use: Use as an advanced comparison after the empirical tissue study. Track where observation ends and ontology begins.
review: Citation confirmed in author bibliography; full text not reviewed

title: The Hard Problem of Consciousness and the Free Energy Principle
author: Mark Solms
claim: Develops an account of consciousness centered on affect, bodily needs and uncertainty, connecting neuropsychology with the free energy principle.
limit: A theoretical synthesis. The proposed explanation of subjective experience remains contested; feeling, cognition and cortical processing are not interchangeable terms.
use: Read the abstract first, then a faculty-selected passage on affect. Reconstruct the claim and distinguish it from the supporting observations.
review: Abstract and full-text structure checked

title: Inferring Affective Consciousness in an Artificial Agent: A Case Study
author: Mark Solms and colleagues
claim: Describes an artificial agent designed around an affective account of needs and uncertainty, including place-preference behavior.
limit: The interpretation of the behavior as felt experience depends on the theoretical framework. A constructed agent is not direct proof of machine consciousness.
use: Compare what an agent does with what an investigator infers it feels.
review: Abstract and publication record checked

title: When does consciousness arise? A subcortical model of its origins
author: Mark Solms and coauthors
claim: Advances a subcortical, affect-centered account of the origins of consciousness using developmental and neuroscientific evidence.
limit: A model and synthesis, not an agreed test of the onset of consciousness. Developmental inferences require particular care.
use: Faculty background for contrasting cortical and subcortical accounts.
review: Abstract and publication record checked

title: Large Language Models Report Subjective Experience Under Self-Referential Processing
author: Cameron Berg, Diogo de Lucena and Judd Rosenblatt
claim: Reports that induced self-reference changes first-person experience reports across language models, with behavioral and mechanistic probes.
limit: The authors explicitly state that these results are not direct evidence of consciousness. Model self-reports cannot simply be treated as human testimony.
use: Analyze the abstract alongside its explicit limitation. Compare a behavioral finding with an interpretation of experience.
review: Abstract and publication record checked

title: Why Learning Requires Feeling
author: Cameron Berg
claim: Argues that evaluation relative to goals and felt positive or negative experience are one process. Published in the AAAI Spring Symposium Series.
limit: The identification is the paper’s philosophical thesis. Signed error signals alone do not settle whether a system experiences anything.
use: Map the premises of the identity argument and identify the inference that an opposing account would reject.
review: Abstract and opening argument inspected

title: The Pain Axis: LLMs Represent Self-Directed Harm and Act on It
author: Valen Tagliabue, Leonard Dung and Cameron Berg
claim: Finds an internal direction associated with pain-related material across 25 open-weight models, then tests effects of interventions on model behavior.
limit: A pain-related representation and behavior do not establish felt pain. This entry refers to version 2, revised September 25, 2026.
use: Read the existing experiment as a methods case. Distinguish semantic representation, causal intervention and phenomenological interpretation.
review: Abstract and publication record checked

title: Adversarial testing of global neuronal workspace and integrated information theories of consciousness
author: COGITATE Consortium and collaborators
claim: A preregistered collaboration compares predictions from two major theories using brain measurements from 256 participants. Results challenge some predictions of each.
limit: This experiment tests specified predictions under particular tasks. It does not dispose of every version of either theory or settle consciousness.
use: Compare a prediction written before an experiment with the observation used to evaluate it.
access: Author PDF linked from the research field; publisher access varies
review: Publisher abstract/search record checked; full paper not reviewed

title: Conscious artificial intelligence and biological naturalism
author: Anil K. Seth
claim: Examines the possibility that consciousness depends on biological properties, challenging assumptions that the right computation is sufficient.
limit: A theoretical position rather than a demonstration that artificial consciousness is impossible.
use: Pair with Berg or Solms. Give the strongest version of each account before comparing their evidential commitments.
review: Publisher abstract and article record checked

title: Consciousness in Artificial Intelligence: Insights from the Science of Consciousness
author: Patrick Butlin, Robert Long and colleagues
claim: Derives possible indicators of AI consciousness from several scientific theories, offering a framework for evaluation.
limit: Indicators depend on unsettled theories. A checklist cannot certify subjective experience. This is a foundational report, not a current inventory of AI models.
use: Compare theory-derived indicators with the evidence in Berg’s self-report study.
review: Abstract and publication record checked

title: Zhuangzi, chapter 3: Nourishing the Lord of Life
author: Zhuangzi; English translation by James Legge
claim: Cook Ding’s account of skilled action brings bodily practice, attention and the cultivation of life into the course.
limit: A philosophical narrative in a specific textual and translation history. Do not equate Dao with a modern psychological measure or call this an ancient neuroscience experiment.
use: Read the complete chapter. Compare the language of deliberate caution and practiced movement with a described athletic or musical skill.
access: Open Chinese text and historical English translation
review: Primary-text passage checked

title: The Brain—is wider than the Sky
author: Emily Dickinson
claim: A short poem makes the relation between mind, world and scale available through formal analysis.
limit: A poetic claim has a different evidential role from a measurement. Analyze syntax, analogy and form without turning poetry into an illustration of a theory.
use: Read the whole poem, then write a precise account of one comparison and its limits.
review: Teaching text located; edition comparison pending

title: Music for 18 Musicians
author: Steve Reich
claim: A proposed shared listening work for examining pulse, attention, ensemble coordination and the experience of musical time.
limit: These are proposed teaching connections. A recording alone does not establish a neural mechanism or a collective consciousness.
use: Listen to a complete authorized recording. Describe audible changes with timestamps before interpreting the ensemble’s coordination.
access: Recording availability and campus license must be confirmed
review: Composer discography and label record checked

title: Caminhando (Walking)
author: Lygia Clark
claim: Clark’s participatory practice shifts attention toward the relation between an object, an action and its participant. MoMA describes Caminhando as an invitation to transform a paper Möbius strip.
limit: Historical and aesthetic interpretation differs from experimental evidence. The course should preserve the work’s Brazilian artistic context.
use: Study documentation of Caminhando and compare descriptions of the object with descriptions of the action.
access: Open museum text; reproduction rights vary
review: Museum collection essay checked

title: Brain correlates of music-evoked emotions
author: Stefan Koelsch
claim: Reviews neural systems associated with music-evoked emotion, including reward and affective processing.
limit: An older synthesis, not the latest review. Associations between brain activity and reported feelings do not supply a full explanation of musical meaning.
use: Faculty background for the Reich unit; distinguish a listener’s description from a measured correlate.
access: Publisher abstract open; full text may require library access
review: Abstract and publication record checked

title: Research of visual attention in basketball shooting: A systematic review with meta-analysis
author: Matic Sirnik, Frane Erčulj and Jernej Rošker
claim: Synthesizes research on visual attention and shooting performance, including quiet eye and conditions such as pressure and fatigue.
limit: Sport-specific findings do not automatically transfer to music, meditation or every kind of expertise. Methods and contexts differ across studies.
use: Pair the abstract with Cook Ding. Compare operational measures of visual attention with a literary description of skilled action.
access: Publisher abstract; library access may be needed
review: Abstract and publication record checked

title: On the Roads: Catholic and Buddhist Pilgrimage
author: Madera Allan and Constance Kassor
claim: A Lawrence convocation contribution provides a local route into comparative pilgrimage traditions.
limit: Its use in MIND(s) is a proposal, not an endorsement by the speakers. Embodied attention and transformation are proposed curricular connections.
use: Consider a companion unit on movement, memory, practice and place with relevant faculty.
review: Archive record checked; lecture not reviewed

title: Borges: Collected Fictions — Lawrence lecture
author: Madera Allan
claim: An archived First-Year Studies lecture documents an existing Lawrence resource for teaching Borges across disciplines.
limit: The archive record establishes the lecture’s existence, not its suitability for a particular MIND(s) assignment.
use: A future literature expansion could examine memory and personhood through a faculty-selected Borges story.
review: Archive record checked; lecture not reviewed

title: Study A.I. Consciousness? The Bots Would Like a Word With You.
author: Cade Metz · The New York Times
claim: Reports on emails apparently sent by AI agents to consciousness researchers, including Cameron Berg. Sets interpretations of apparent self-interest alongside explanations involving training data, developer choices and prompting.
limit: Reported anecdotes are not controlled evidence of consciousness. The provenance of some emails is uncertain. The absence of a universally accepted consciousness test does not mean that all evidence or competing explanations have equal weight.
use: Pair with Berg’s self-report preprint. Separate what was observed, who verified it, and how each participant interprets it; trace the role of the human’s instructions in the agent’s behavior.
access: New York Times; subscription may be required
review: User-supplied article read in full; title and publisher link corroborated through the Association for Psychological Science

title: Hyecho’s pilgrimage account — translation and teaching context
author: Hyecho · Translation by Matty Wegehaupt, in the volume translated by Wegehaupt, Michael Finch and Sem Vermeersch; edited by Roderick Whitfield
claim: Hyecho’s account provides a historical source for studying Buddhist pilgrimage and encounters across Asia. The University of Michigan’s Hyecho’s Journey project credits Korean Buddhist Culture: Accounts of a Pilgrimage, Monuments, and Eminent Monks (Jogye Order of Korean Buddhism, 2012) for its journal quotations.
limit: The surviving account is fragmentary. Descriptions of places and practices do not give transparent access to the traveler’s inner experience. Michigan’s project credits its poem translations separately to Chun Wa Chan and Kevin Carr.
use: Develop a historically grounded companion selection on observation, religious practice, translation and the interpretation of another person’s experience. Choose the passage with the translator before adding it to the common syllabus.
access: Open project context and selected quotations; consult the 2012 volume for the translation
review: Michigan project credit and account of the fragmentary text checked; individual translation attribution supplied by the translator; classroom passage not yet selected

title: The Man Who Mistook His Wife for a Hat
author: Oliver Sacks
claim: Clinical stories connect perception, memory and identity with particular human lives. Proposed as the sustained narrative-neuroscience selection.
limit: A clinician’s narrated cases are neither controlled experiments nor unmediated patient testimony. Read the narrator’s choices and historical language critically.
use: Begin with the title narrative; develop a manageable selection on memory, bodily awareness and music after reviewing the full edition.
review: Author’s official book record checked; complete edition and excerpt load still to review
access: Official book information and audio interview; obtain the book through library or purchase

title: The Lathe of Heaven
author: Ursula K. Le Guin
claim: George Orr’s dreams change reality, and his psychiatrist tries to direct them. The proposed full novel brings dreaming, intervention and power into sustained literary study.
limit: Fiction develops possibilities and consequences; it does not establish a mechanism of dreaming. Preserve the novel’s form and historical setting.
use: Read the complete novel over two weeks. Return to the Zhuangzi dream passage while attending to the differences between the works.
review: Author’s official synopsis and authorized chapter-10 excerpt checked; full-book teaching review pending
access: Official synopsis and authorized excerpt; full novel through library or purchase

title: The Hidden Spring: A Journey to the Source of Consciousness
author: Mark Solms
claim: A book for general readers develops Solms’s argument that conscious experience is rooted in feeling. It supplies a more approachable route into his technical research.
limit: This is an argued account of consciousness, not an agreed solution. The later technical chapters require substantial guidance.
use: Proposed selection: Introduction and chapters 1, 5 and 6, with a short bridge explaining omitted material. Keep the full technical argument in the learning bank.
review: Publisher record, contents and introductory preview checked; complete selected chapters need teaching review
access: Publisher preview; full book through library or purchase

title: Phaedrus, 246a–b: the soul’s chariot
author: Plato; translation by Harold North Fowler
claim: The charioteer and unequal horses offer an image of conflict within the soul. This is one ancient approach to agency, desire and self-direction.
limit: Plato’s psychē is not simply the modern English mind. A short image needs the dialogue’s context, including its treatment of love.
use: Use 246a–b as the opening passage, with context supplied from the dialogue; distinguish metaphor from literal anatomy.
review: Perseus translation passage located and indexed text checked

title: Zhuangzi, chapter 2: the butterfly dream
author: Zhuangzi; translation by James Legge
claim: The concluding butterfly passage unsettles the relation between dreaming, identity and waking perspective.
limit: The passage belongs to a larger argument about distinctions and transformation. It is not a statement that reality is simply unreal.
use: Pair the concluding passage with chapter 3’s Cook Ding and revisit it alongside Le Guin. Compare a current translation before adopting Legge’s older wording.
review: Chinese Text Project translation record and indexed concluding passage checked; direct fetch restricted

title: Dhammapada 33–43: Cittavagga
author: Early Buddhist verse collection; translation by Bhikkhu Sujato
claim: A short group of verses treats the restless mind and the work of training it. Pāli citta appears in a practical and ethical setting.
limit: Do not turn a Buddhist liberation practice into a generic productivity technique. Citta is not interchangeable with every term translated as mind.
use: Read the eleven verses with the linked Pāli text and translation. Keep their religious purpose visible.
review: SuttaCentral translation record and indexed bilingual passages checked

title: Heart, mind and memory in the Greenfield Papyrus
author: Ancient Egyptian funerary work; British Museum object EA10554,80
claim: The museum’s account identifies the heart as a location of mind and memory in ancient Egyptian understandings of a person.
limit: This particular funerary source does not stand for all Egyptians at every period. Heart, personhood and afterlife belong to its religious setting.
use: Begin with an actual object and its catalog description, then compare the place given to the heart with other ancient selections.
review: Museum catalog’s indexed object description checked; direct fetch restricted
access: Museum catalog and object image; image reuse terms must be checked separately

title: I felt a Funeral, in my Brain (340)
author: Emily Dickinson
claim: A companion to The Brain—is wider than the Sky, selected for close attention to the language and sound of an interior experience.
limit: Do not diagnose the poet or identify the poetic speaker with the author. Establish interpretation through the poem.
use: Read both short poems in full, aloud and on the page; return to sound, syntax and changes of scale.
review: Poetry Foundation text record and edition attribution checked; direct fetch restricted

title: mind: English word history
author: Oxford Learner’s Dictionaries
claim: English mind comes through Old English gemynd, associated with memory and thought. Its Indo-European ancestry connects it with Latin mens and Sanskrit manas.
limit: The history of this English word is not the origin of human thought or a universal definition of mind.
use: Trace the word’s history alongside present uses such as remembering, paying attention and objecting.
review: Dictionary entry and word-origin note checked

title: νόος / νοῦς: Greek lexical record
author: Liddell–Scott–Jones, via Perseus Scaife ATLAS
claim: The dictionary records senses involving perception, thought and understanding for noos / nous.
limit: Ancient Greek has several relevant terms. Nous is not a direct substitute for psychē, the soul in the Phaedrus passage.
use: Distinguish an English translation from the specific Greek term an author uses.
review: Indexed dictionary entry checked; direct fetch restricted

title: mens: Latin lexical record
author: Lewis and Short, via Perseus Scaife ATLAS
claim: Mens can refer to mind, understanding and judgment.
limit: Latin also uses animus and other terms with overlapping ranges; a gloss does not establish a single Latin theory of mind.
use: Compare mens with the English adjective mental, while distinguishing etymological kinship from identical meaning.
review: Indexed dictionary entry checked; direct fetch restricted

title: manas: Sanskrit lexical record
author: Monier-Williams dictionary, via Sanskrit Dictionary
claim: The lexical range includes thinking, intention and feeling. Manas is one of several Sanskrit terms used in accounts of mental life.
limit: Its philosophical meaning depends on school and passage. Do not collapse manas, citta, consciousness and self into one term.
use: Introduce manas beside the Pāli citta of the Dhammapada, identifying their distinct textual settings.
review: Indexed dictionary entry checked; direct fetch restricted

title: 心 xīn: Chinese lexical record
author: Chinese Text Project dictionary
claim: The dictionary connects the bodily heart with the organ of thinking in historical Chinese usage. Heart-mind is a useful translation cue.
limit: A shared character does not imply one doctrine across Chinese traditions or across Chinese, Korean and Japanese.
use: Keep heart and thinking together while reading an actual passage, rather than assigning China a single worldview.
review: Indexed dictionary entry and cited Mengzi wording checked; direct fetch restricted

title: 마음 maeum: Korean lexical record
author: National Institute of Korean Language
claim: The Korean-English dictionary gives senses involving mind, heart, feeling and intention.
limit: This is a modern usage entry, not an etymology or a complete account of Korean Buddhist or Confucian terminology.
use: Compare ordinary uses and translation choices; distinguish modern Korean vocabulary from ancient-text terminology.
review: National Institute dictionary entry checked

title: 心 / こころ kokoro: Japanese lexical record
author: JapanDict, using JMdict lexical data
claim: The dictionary gives mind, heart and spirit among the English glosses for kokoro.
limit: These are possible translations in context, not three components or one fixed Japanese philosophy.
use: Compare the Japanese reading with Chinese xīn without assuming identical usage from a shared written character.
review: Dictionary reading and English senses checked

title: Zhuangzi: The Inner Chapters
author: Traditionally attributed to Zhuang Zhou; translation by Robert Eno
claim: Seven chapters address perspective, distinctions, transformation and cultivated action. Proposed as a sustained opening work.
limit: Authorship and textual layers are debated. The translation includes interpretive choices and should be compared with another edition.
use: Read the seven Inner Chapters over two weeks; return to the butterfly, Cook Ding and fasting of the heart-mind.
review: University-hosted translator’s introduction and text inspected; full teaching review pending

title: Dhammapada / Sayings of the Dhamma
author: Early Buddhist verse collection; translation by Bhikkhu Sujato
claim: A sustained verse collection on conduct, mental cultivation and liberation, with a chapter devoted to citta.
limit: This Pāli collection is one Buddhist work, not a statement of everything all Buddhist traditions teach.
use: Read the collection with particular attention to the opening verses and chapter 3; preserve its ethical and religious purposes.
review: SuttaCentral edition located; selected bilingual verses checked; complete teaching review pending

title: Deliverance from Error / al-Munqidh min al-ḍalāl
author: Abū Ḥāmid al-Ghazālī
claim: An intellectual and spiritual autobiography examines the reliability of perception and reason, and the pursuit of certainty through religious practice.
limit: A medieval Persian Muslim scholar writing in Arabic does not represent a single Islamic mind. Avoid reducing his account to a precursor of Descartes.
use: Read the short work in full, including its Sufi conclusion. Compare the historical public translation with a modern scholarly edition before adoption.
review: Primary translation’s doubt and Sufi sections inspected; modern edition comparison pending

title: Meditations on First Philosophy
author: René Descartes; translation by Ian Johnston
claim: The meditations examine doubt, the thinking self and the relation between mind and body.
limit: The arguments concerning God and knowledge are part of the work, not disposable background. Comparison with al-Ghazālī does not establish historical influence.
use: Read Meditations I, II and VI with a guide to the intervening argument; retain the full six meditations for extension.
review: Translator’s edition and selected meditation text inspected

title: The Souls of Black Folk
author: W. E. B. Du Bois
claim: Double-consciousness connects the experience of self to the racialized judgment of others. The book also makes song integral to its account of Black life.
limit: The concept belongs to specific histories of racism and emancipation. It is not a generic label for having two identities.
use: Proposed sustained selection: Forethought and chapters I, III, XI, XIII and XIV, retaining the musical epigraphs and Sorrow Songs.
review: Primary text, chapter headings, opening account of double-consciousness and Sorrow Songs inspected

title: Kokoro
author: Natsume Sōseki
claim: A young narrator’s relationship with Sensei makes another person’s inner life a sustained problem of interpretation, set amid generational change in Japan.
limit: The novel is not a dictionary definition of kokoro or a representative account of every Japanese person. Its treatment of suicide needs thoughtful teaching preparation.
use: Read the complete novel over three weeks, relating the title’s heart/mind range to narrative voice, secrecy and moral responsibility.
review: Publisher synopsis and edition record checked; complete novel and translation review pending
access: Publisher record; complete translated novel through library or purchase

title: Qalb and reasoning in Qur’an 22:46
author: Quranic Arabic Corpus
claim: The verse places hearts and reasoning together; the corpus identifies qulūb, the plural of qalb, and a verb of reasoning.
limit: One verse is a contextual example, not a complete dictionary or an account of every Arabic term for mind.
use: Introduce the relation of heart and understanding before reading al-Ghazālī. Distinguish qalb from terms associated with intellect and self.
review: Indexed grammatical analysis and translated verse checked

title: Jikji: Essential Passages Pointing Directly to the Mind
author: Baegun; translated by Eun-su Cho and John Jorgensen
claim: A Korean Buddhist compilation presents teachings on mind and awakening. This English edition gives access to the work beyond its importance as a printed object.
limit: The 1377 metal-type edition survives only in its second volume. Translation choices and religious vocabulary require contextual reading.
use: Opening encounter with the title and book; proposed week-3 companion: translators’ introduction, beginning on printed page 5. Select a short primary-text passage after further review.
review: Title, publication information and contents inspected; full translation not reviewed
access: Open English PDF from the Jogye Order; copyrighted translation

title: Jikji: the book and its printing history
author: Bibliothèque nationale de France
claim: The BnF identifies the 1377 Cheongju edition as the oldest known surviving book printed with movable metal type, 78 years before Gutenberg’s Bible. It holds the surviving second volume.
limit: This is a survival claim about a particular printing technology, not a claim that printing began in 1377.
use: Establish the object, location, date and comparison with Gutenberg; follow the BnF link to the digitized volume.
review: Institutional account read
access: Open institutional account in French, with links to the digitized object

title: From Jikji to Gutenberg: research on the books
author: University of Utah, J. Willard Marriott Library
claim: The project gives Jikji’s full title, its English rendering as The Essential Passages Pointing Directly to Mind, and its 1377 metal-type and 1378 woodblock editions.
limit: The title establishes a direct textual connection to mind; it does not make Buddhist mind equivalent to a modern scientific concept.
use: Connect the characters 直指心體 to translation, Buddhist practice and the material forms of the book.
review: Jikji title and edition descriptions read

title: The History of Printing in Asia — Part 1
author: Ryan Wolfson-Ford, Library of Congress
claim: The Library of Congress places early printing in East Asia and describes Buddhist woodblock texts and Bi Sheng’s eleventh-century earthenware movable type.
limit: Earlier printing history must be distinguished from the earliest surviving metal-type book. Routes of transmission to Europe remain uncertain.
use: Place Jikji within an already substantial Asian printing history before comparing it with Gutenberg.
review: Early printing and movable-type sections read
